paras: The killing of John Lowery was the fatal shooting of a Black miner, John Lowery (also spelled Lowry), by Policeman Harry Messer at Keystone, West Virginia, on the night of August 1, 1900. Messer, who according to the dispatches had been attacked by Lowery with a knife, was reportedly acquitted as acting in self-defence at Welch the next day. Papers across the country reported it because Black residents, said to be a majority of the town, threatened to lynch the officer, and headlines warned of a "race war" among the coal miners.

Keystone was a coal-mining town near Welch where Black residents were "a majority of the population." According to a special dispatch printed in the Louisville Courier-Journal and the Morgantown Daily New Dominion, trouble had existed for weeks between Black and white residents, with "numerous fights" having occurred.

On the night of August 1, "half a dozen black and white miners" were fighting in the suburbs of Keystone when Messer tried to arrest "a negro" (in the Courier-Journal, "the colored men," which he was "powerless" to do). In this version Lowery turned on the policeman with a knife, and Messer fired twice, killing him instantly. A special to the Wheeling Register from Welch described the shooting differently: Messer "was attacked and compelled to open fire on the crowd," killing Lowry and slightly injuring another man. The Associated Press report said only that officers, "in quelling a disturbance," killed one Black man and injured several others.

The shooting angered Black residents, and a crowd started for Messer, who escaped to a hotel. The Sun and the Courier-Journal said Sheriff White and a dozen armed men guarded him there overnight; the Register placed him at his boarding house under "a strong guard." For an hour some fifty Black men paraded the streets threatening to lynch Messer, "hurling insults at all the whites of that vicinity," in the Courier-Journal's words; the Register said the parading lasted most of the night.

On the morning of August 2 many Black miners refused to go to work, and correspondents wrote that more serious trouble was feared. The Associated Press added that Black residents were holding indignation meetings. Messer was taken to Welch that day; the Register said he went for a preliminary hearing, and the Sun and the Washington Times reported that he was acquitted on the ground that he killed Lowery "purely in self-defence."

White residents, the Register said, claimed they were "amply able to cope with any difficulty that may arise." No report of an inquest, a grand jury inquiry or later trouble at Keystone appears in the coverage.

Most readers learned of the shooting through a short Associated Press brief, dated Keystone, August 2, carried on August 3 by papers from the Indianapolis Journal to the Saint Paul Globe and as late as August 11 by the Buffalo Voice of Wyoming. It named no one; headlines read "Race War Among Coal Miners" and "Miners' Race War Feared."

A longer special, which named Messer and Lowery, ran in the Sun under "Negroes After a White Man," in the Courier-Journal under "Negroes Up in Arms," and in the Morgantown Daily New Dominion under a deck saying the officer had to be protected "from Being Lynched." The Washington Times headed the same text "Policeman Shoots a Vicious Negro in Self-Defence," presenting the officer's account as fact. The Wheeling Register gave its Welch special the headline "Race War Is On at Keystone," with decks saying the shooting "rouses negro miners to violence" and that the officer "was compelled to open fire."

Roundup columns in Ohio and Virginia papers shrank the story to a threatened race war, the Clarke Courier saying Black residents were threatening "to lynch the policeman and all whites." Every account came from white newspapers, none quoting a Black witness, and no Black-press coverage of the shooting was found.

Besides differing on how the shooting happened and how many were hurt, the detailed specials place it on the night of August 1, while the AP brief says "to-day," August 2; the specials, one from nearby Welch, are the better evidence on timing. Only the Sun and Washington Times report the acquittal.

reader.title: Killing of John Lowery
bases: A policeman, Harry Messer, shot and killed John Lowery while trying to make an arrest during a fight among miners; no mob or posse took part in the killing (A3, A4, A6).

Three independent reports (the AP brief A2/A8, the special in A3/A4/A5, and the Wheeling Register's Welch special A6) agree that an officer shot and killed a Black miner at Keystone, though they differ on how.

framing.detail: AP brief under headlines such as 'Race War Among Coal Miners' and 'Miners' Race War Feared', giving no names and treating the killing as 'quelling a disturbance'.
The special presented the knife attack and self-defence as fact; the Washington Times headed it 'Policeman Shoots a Vicious Negro in Self-Defence' and the Sun 'Negroes After a White Man'.
The Wheeling Register's decks said the shooting 'rouses negro miners to violence' and that the officer 'was compelled to open fire'.
Roundup briefs reduced the story to a threatened race war after a policeman or 'white officer' killed a negro miner.
